newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Cargill sees growing Asian role in rubber pricing.
newsitem.headline: Cargill sees growing Asian role in rubber pricing.

text.p: Asia's role in setting rubber prices is likely to grow strongly by 2000 because of the projected sharp growth in its synthetic rubber output, an executive from private U.S. trader Cargill said on Thursday.

Michael Coleman, managing director of Cargill's rubber and latex division, told the Asia Rubber Markets conference in Singapore that Asia's synthetic rubber production, outside Japan, could rise to 3.5 million tonnes by 2000 from 2.7 million tonnes in 1995.

Approximately 10.3 million tonnes of the total world supply of 17.5 million tonnes of rubber in 2000 will come from Asia, he said. The region will produce about 6.85 million tonnes of natural rubber. Asian rubber consumption at that time will be 8.3 million tonnes, Coleman added.
"This expected concentration of both supply and demand within Asia will ensure that the primary arena for price discovery and price establishment will be within Asia," he said.
"We can certainly expect to see Asian production, consumption and trade flows exerting an increasing influence on global synthetic rubber prices," he added.

India's synthetic rubber capacity was expected to rise by up to 400,000 tonnes a year by 2000, South Korea's by 130,000 tonnes, Thailand's by 300,000 tonnes, Indonesia's by 200,000 tonnes and China's also by 200,000 tonnes, Coleman said.
"Over the longer term, it seems likely that Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam will also develop synthetic rubber capacities," he said.
Cargill expected the dominance of the three major natural rubber producers -- Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia -- to continue.
"Over the next five years, nothing will change this position," Coleman said.
But a long-term shift in production is underway as the focus of production expands in South Sumatra and Kalimantan in Indonesia and in Indochina.
"Indochina will become a major producer," Coleman said, adding that there may be a slackening in Thai output and Malaysia's decline may become irreversible.
